concept.name: Volatility arbitrage
concept.definition: A class of option-based relative-value strategies that trade the difference between an option's implied volatility and a forecast of the underlying's future realized volatility, implemented through a delta-neutral portfolio of options and the underlying. The trader treats volatility, rather than price, as the unit of relative value: buying options delta-hedged is a bet that realized volatility will exceed implied, and selling them is the opposite bet.
concept.intuition: If the market is pricing options as if the stock will move 10% but you think it will move 20%, you can buy the options, hedge out the direction, and profit from the extra movement itself.
concept.mechanics: Forecast realized volatility (e.g., from historical or high-frequency returns), compare with implied volatility backed out of market option prices, then buy underpriced or sell overpriced options and keep the book delta-neutral by trading the underlying. Profit is realized through the continuous re-hedging (gamma scalping) of the position over the option's life.
concept.formula: Option value C = f(S, sigma, ...); implied volatility sigma_imp solves C_market = f(S, sigma_imp, ...). Trade long vol if sigma_imp < sigma_forecast, short vol if sigma_imp > sigma_forecast.
concept.failure_modes: It is not true arbitrage: the forecast can be wrong, and volatility spikes correlated across markets (black-swan events) cause losses across a whole book, as with LTCM's short-volatility positions.
concept.misconceptions: That delta-hedging removes all risk; a delta-neutral book still carries gamma, vega, theta, and jump risk, and 'buying vol cheap' loses steadily through theta if the realized move never comes.
concept.example: A trader buys S&P 500 straddles at 12% implied volatility while forecasting 18% realized, delta-hedging daily; if realized vol comes in near 18%, the re-hedging gains exceed the theta paid.
